name: What to Measure
title: What to Measure
answer: The measure most AI pilots reach for, how often a tool was opened or how many prompts were typed, shows only that people used it, not that anything improved. What to measure should follow from the problem the pilot was meant to solve, whether that is teacher time or student learning. Every pilot should also count governance incidents, because a tool that works but causes harm is not a success.

sections.body: Usage counts are the most common measure in AI pilots and the least useful, because logins, minutes of use and prompt numbers only show that the tool was opened. A tool can be used constantly and still change nothing about learning or workload, and heavy use can hide the problem of students leaning on it and learning less. The measure has to match the problem the pilot set out to solve. If the goal was saving teacher time, the measure is minutes saved per week, followed by a question about where those minutes went. If the goal was learning, the measure is learning on a task done without the tool, compared with a classroom that did not use it.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: A school picks its measure from the problem it named before the pilot began. A pilot aimed at teacher workload counts minutes saved each week and then traces where the freed time actually went, since saved time can be absorbed by other demands. A pilot aimed at learning sets a task done without the tool and compares it with a classroom that did not use it. Figure 4.6 lists eight kinds of measures with an example of each, and most pilots should choose one main measure plus one or two supporting ones. The text does not set these measures out by grade band.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text reports three findings. One study found that teachers who cut their planning time in half saw the saved time absorbed by other demands (Carson et al., 2026). A review of automatic feedback found that nearly half of the studies showed no reduction in teacher workload at all (Cavalcanti et al., 2021). A review of AI in math found an average effect that researchers classify as small (Yi et al., 2024), and the text adds that realistic effects are usually small and can still be worth having at low cost. Figure 4.6 lists eight kinds of measures with an example of each, and the text does not attach an evidence label to this idea.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits here are about honesty and about harm. Usage numbers can make a pilot look successful while nothing improved, and high usage can mask students learning less. Saved teacher time is not automatically a gain, because it can be absorbed by other demands, and automatic feedback does not reliably reduce workload. Every pilot should count governance incidents such as privacy problems or reports of harm, since a tool that works but causes harm is not a success whatever its other numbers say. Choosing which measure matters, and deciding what counts as success, stays with the people running the pilot.
